reference_contexts: Risks Industry Competition- Moderate Risk The primary risk for any restaurant stock is that it ceases to have the most relevant food and environment for changing consumer preferences. The restaurant industry is one of the most challenging, and it requires good management to keep a tight ship and to continually update the menu and environment in order to maintain strong customer traffic. The company updates their menu twice per year, including pricing changes, and in response to criticism about their large portion sizes, The Cheesecake Factory has introduced what they refer to as a SkinnyLicious menu subset that focuses on lower-calorie portions. With Cheesecake Factory Inc’s strong management team, and with the added diversification of North Italia and other brands within Fox Restaurant Concepts, I believe that the company is well-protected from some of the more negative scenarios that restaurants can face. However, it’s always a risk worth monitoring. Margin Pressure- Major Risk Cheesecake Factory’s international licensed locations offer high margins, but their company-operated locations, which represent the bulk of their revenue, have been under margin pressure. Labor costs have been increasing but the company has been slow to raise menu prices. Operating margins reached a peak of 8.8% in 2016 but are currently as low as 5.9%. The growth of North Italia, with its significant alcohol mix leading to 35% cash-on-cash return potential per location, may help to offset these margin pressures as that chain becomes a larger portion of the overall company. Executive Retention- Moderate Risk As previously described, Cheesecake Factory Inc has been well-managed by its co-founder, David Overton, since 1992. He is currently 73, which means he could potentially have a decade or more leading the company ahead of him, or could retire at any time. The company has a strong executive team with long tenures at the company, but losing a co-founder as its long-time CEO would bring about transition risk. Specifically, there’s always a risk with new non-founder management that the company could lose its long-term focus and become more “corporate” with an increased focus on quarterly results and executive compensation, rather than focusing on the long-term process of building a successful company as they have been doing. On the flip side, fresh management at the top might help the company boost margins. For example, they might decide to streamline The Cheesecake Factory’s massive menu, which it seems to me as a customer/investor is something that is at least worth exploring. In addition, Cheesecake Factory Inc recently acquired Fox Restaurant Concepts, which is reliant on Sam Fox’s expertise. Fox is now leading this segment as an independent subsidiary of Cheesecake Factory Inc, and he has a proven track record of successful restaurant concepts. If he were to leave the company, it would bring about significant transition risk for this smaller but promising segment of the overall company. Economic Cycle- Moderate Risk Restaurant sales are moderately affected by the economic cycle. People eat out less, and may choose less expensive options, during recessionary periods. The U.S. restaurant industry is healthy and growing, with about $55 billion in revenue per month: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed Industry-wide revenue grows by about 5% per year on average, but during the severe recession of 2008/2009, the year-over-year industry growth briefly dropped to about -2%: Chart Source: St. Louis Fed This doesn’t seem like much, but it can have a substantial impact on operating margins, which are only 5-8% for a company like Cheesecake Factory Inc. For the full year 2018, the company’s earnings per share were already down 14% from their 2016 highs, and is what led to a significant part of the stock’s recent decline. This is a risk worth factoring into growth rates, and is one reason why I instantly knocked down the company’s 8% target revenue growth to a baseline estimate of 6%. Growing by 8% represents an ideal potential year, where the industry is great and the company executes its new growth strategy well. Any long-term growth period, however, needs to assume that a recession occurs somewhere in there, severely throwing off expected growth numbers for a year or two. Stock Market Selloff- Moderate Risk Regardless of economic and earnings performance, Cheesecake’s stock could easily be subject to a sell-off should the S&P 500 face a severe correction. reference: Mexico is grouped among the more troubled emerging markets. The report notes that financial conditions vary significantly by nation within emerging markets: some, such as Taiwan and Thailand, are described as financially stable, while others, including Argentina, Indonesia, and Mexico, are characterized as more troubled. This distinction is made in the context of a global financial system that is about to be tested in both anticipated and unanticipated ways, amid record-high debt levels, flat corporate profit growth in 2019, and economic indicators pointing flat or down even before the coronavirus and the quarantine response accelerated the downturn.
reference_contexts: Market Crash Deep Dive Analysis Published March 15, 2020 This past week has been one of the most historic weeks in global stock market history, on par in terms of volatility with 2008, 1987, or 1929. Rather than do a deep dive on an individual stock as usual, this report’s deep dive will be on the whole macro situation along with several stock examples, due to the unprecedented market situation. Nobody has the full picture including me, and in this environment anything can happen, but a lot of the things we’ve been tracking for a couple years now, in my free newsletters and articles, and more recently in this premium research service, are coming home to roost and these are key turning points to see how they turn out. The main surprise is that it’s all happening faster than expected, accelerated by the coronavirus and more specifically the quarantine response to it. There’s often a curve ball or black swan somewhere, and this time it was a virus. Many pundits on CNBC and other media outlets seem to think that the economy was doing just fine before this hit, but that was not the case. Corporate profit growth was 0% in 2019, and excluding buybacks and tax cuts has been flat for several years before the involvement of trade wars or viruses. Most year-over-year economic indicators were pointing flat or down. Debt levels are near record highs, and the bottom half of the U.S. population is deeply financially insecure, more than they have been historically. The U.S. government deficit as a percentage of GDP has been rising dramatically since 2016; it’s supposed to shrink during a strong economy. Europe and Japan are better or worse in some ways, with even higher total debt levels but more financially secure people in the lower income levels. Germany has had a government budget surplus from which it can now draw from. With emerging markets, it varies significantly depending on the specific nation. Some are financially stable, like Taiwan or Thailand, while others like Argentina, Indonesia, and Mexico are more troubled. This situation will put the global financial system to the test in ways we saw coming, and in ways we won’t. For example, Thailand is in financially good shape with large financial reserves, but is heavily reliant on $60+ billion/year in tourism revenue, which is drying up from this virus more than it would in a normal recession. Many U.S. restaurants are in decent shape financially, but can they handle months with limited customers, in a far deeper restaurant sales decline than a normal recession? We’ll see. The Systemic Debt Issue The United States reached a peak total debt (public + private) at 380% of GDP in 2009. That was our all-time record high. More specifically, the U.S. entered that recession with a total debt/GDP ratio of a bit under 350%, and it grew to 380% during the process. After a period of modest deleveraging, mainly in the housing sector, we’re currently back down to just under 350% debt to GDP. So, we’re entering this likely recession with a similar level of debt as 2007. Specifically, we have way higher government debt, as well as higher consumer credit and corporate debt, but lower mortgage debt compared to that time, as a percentage of GDP. The third highest debt level ever reached was back in the Great Depression that started in 1929. In the early 1930’s at its peak, we reached 300% debt to GDP. It’s too far back to be on the St. Louis Fed chart above, but there are other data sources that recorded it. In fourth place was the 2001 recession, which was entered with about 275% debt to GDP. Debt magnifies everything, and is a big variable for what makes some recessions worse than others. The Great Depression of 1929 and the Great Recession of 2008 were so severe in part because debt levels were so historically high. Those two periods are “special” in terms of how rapidly the monetary base was expanded to deal with them compared to every other recession. This is a chart of the U.S. monetary base in log form, so every move up is exponential and this makes it easier to see the differences between normal exponential growth and accelerated exponential growth. Those periods from 1930-1950 and 2008-present represent multi-fold increases in the monetary base in a short period of time, while every other recession on the chart looks normal. The zero bound on interest rates was hit in these two major periods, so they just printed money for stimulus instead, roughly speaking. A few years after the initial 1929 crash, the U.S. devalued the dollar and began printing money from 1932 and onward to fund various programs. Then it slowed down, and in 1937 they encountered another recession, which was still within the larger context of the Great Depression period. So they turned on the printing presses again, and kept them on all through WW2. We’re most likely about to mirror that period in the 2020’s in terms of monetary policy (hopefully without the war part). The Great Recession triggered several rounds of exponential monetary base expansion from 2008 to 2014, and then they stopped until 2019. During this next period, we’re about to have another big increase in the monetary base, similar to what happened in 1937. We already started in September 2019 when the repo spike happened and the Fed started monetizing Treasury bills, and it’s likely about to get amplified.

Macro View Liquidity Indicators Domestic liquidity indicators continue to run almost perfectly sideways, in large part because the Treasury and Fed have been in lockstep regarding this: Notably, Stephen Miran and Nouriel Roubini recently published a paper about “Activist Treasury Issuance” which is their term that refers to the Treasury Department taking unusual actions to offset the Fed’s tightness. Both Miran and Roubini are economics PhDs and worked in various capacities with the Treasury Department in the past. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. It’s normal for the Treasury to issue an excessive ratio of T-bills during a crisis such as in 2020, but it’s highly unusual for them to be doing it in relatively benign economic and market conditions like we’ve had over the past couple years. I’d argue that it’s a symptom of the ongoing fiscal dominance that the United States finds itself in. T-bills are more “money-like” than longer duration T-bonds, and so when a government finds itself issuing a ton of debt at a time when neither their central bank nor their primary foreign investors are currently buying that issuance, they can issue more short-duration debt. Short duration debt, being of limited volatility, can be held by investors similar to how they would hold cash. Here’s Miran and Roubini’s executive summary: By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and through them, the economy, usurping core functions of the Federal Reserve. We dub this novel tool “activist Treasury issuance,” or ATI. By manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors, ATI works through the same channels as the Fed’s quantitative easing programs. ATI has been a major market driver over the past year and we expect it will continue to play a significant role in the years ahead; ATI may become a regular element of the policy toolbox, driving political business cycles in the market and the economy. We calculate that ATI has reduced 10-year yields over the last year by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing similar stimulus as a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, the central bank’s primary policy tool. Combined with higher neutral rates, ATI implies the total stance of both monetary and issuance policy, considered together, is roughly neutral—in other words, ATI has interdicted the Fed’s attempt to restrain the economy, helping explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises over the past year. If ATI is unwound via terming out $1 trillion of excess Treasury Bills, we expect it to temporarily boost 10-year yields by 50 basis points, before settling into a permanent 30-bp increase, with corresponding price changes in risk assets. A 50-bp increase in the 10-year yield will have similar economic effects as a two-point hike in the Fed Funds rate. If ATI is not unwound but becomes a permanently employed policy tool, we are likely to see higher equilibrium inflation and interest rates priced in over time due to political business cycles becoming reality. Regular readers of my work will be quite familiar with this concept. I start most of my reports by discussing liquidity conditions, including what the Treasury has been doing with its excess T-bill issuance. And at the start of this year, I dedicated my January 2024 newsletter to this phenomenon of the Treasury offsetting the Fed. Here was a key snippet: Ever since the fourth quarter of 2022, and extending all throughout 2023, the U.S. Federal Reserve and the U.S. Treasury have been operating opposite policies from each other. And the Treasury has had to pull two different levers to keep up with the Fed. -From September 2022 through May 2023, the Treasury drained their own cash reserves back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. -From June 2023 to the present, the Treasury rapidly increased their T-bill issuance as a percentage of their debt issuance and thus drained reverse repos back into the financial system, which offset the Fed. The Fed in blue has been doing its part to reduce liquidity in the financial system since early 2022. The Treasury in red (reflecting both their own cash balances and their ability to affect the reverse repo facility based on their ability to issue T-bills) has been doing its part to increase liquidity in the financial system since late 2022. In the paper, they argued that the Treasury has been shortening the average duration of its debt issuance via excess T-bill issuance, and thus offsetting some of the monetary tightening that the Fed has been doing. T-bills are more “money-like” than longer duration T-bonds, and so when a government finds itself issuing a ton of debt at a time when neither their central bank nor their primary foreign investors are currently buying that issuance, they can issue more short-duration debt. Short duration debt, being of limited volatility, can be held by investors similar to how they would hold cash. Here’s Miran and Roubini’s executive summary: By adjusting the maturity profile of its debt issuance, Treasury is dynamically managing financial conditions and through them, the economy, usurping core functions of the Federal Reserve. We dub this novel tool “activist Treasury issuance,” or ATI. By manipulating the amount of interest rate risk owned by investors, ATI works through the same channels as the Fed’s quantitative easing programs. ATI has been a major market driver over the past year and we expect it will continue to play a significant role in the years ahead; ATI may become a regular element of the policy toolbox, driving political business cycles in the market and the economy. We calculate that ATI has reduced 10-year yields over the last year by roughly a quarter of a percent, providing similar stimulus as a one-point cut in the Fed Funds rate, the central bank’s primary policy tool. Combined with higher neutral rates, ATI implies the total stance of both monetary and issuance policy, considered together, is roughly neutral—in other words, ATI has interdicted the Fed’s attempt to restrain the economy, helping explain inflation persistence and upward nominal growth surprises over the past year. First, with fiscal stimulus being withdrawn and monetary policy tightening, the demand side of the economy became weak, which showed up in poor risk asset performance and contributed to imbalances in the global financial system centered on inflation and currency. Those imbalances (the BOJ pegging 10-year JGBs at 0.25% via unlimited money creation, Europe's self-imposed energy crisis, and China's yuan devaluation) drove foreign currencies lower and pushed the dollar to a new cycle high, stronger than expected. A strong dollar is problematic because the foreign official sector stops buying U.S. Treasuries - they held fewer Treasuries than a year earlier despite record U.S. monthly trade deficits sending them investable dollars. The inverse correlation between dollar strength and foreign demand for Treasuries remains strong, because foreign countries trim Treasuries to buy back and defend their own currencies; they only tend to accumulate Treasuries when the dollar weakens. This matters because falling stock prices reduce federal tax receipts (stock prices are tightly correlated with and lead tax receipts), which widens deficits and requires more Treasury issuance precisely when foreign buyers are absent. The resolution, per the analysis, is that the Fed would be forced to step in and buy Treasuries (a severe degradation of central bank independence during high inflation, similar to the 1940s), or use other levers like the supplementary leverage ratio to get banks to buy more. Ultimately, running loose fiscal policy and tight monetary policy simultaneously is like pressing the gas and brake at once, and monetary policy is expected to blink first and return to structural monetary base expansion, which would take steam out of the dollar index. For bitcoin, the author is bullish on an 18-month view while having no firm view on the next 3-6 months, expecting bitcoin to continue exhibiting a significant degree of correlation with global liquidity indicators - and since liquidity is expected to be higher 18 months out (once the Fed and/or Treasury pivot to maintain Treasury market functioning), that supports the constructive longer-term stance, alongside preferences for short- and intermediate-term Treasuries, inflation-protected Treasuries, gold, and appropriately valued equities over long-duration bonds.

reference: Both episodes involve the removal of a major structural source of bitcoin demand. Earlier in the cycle, when bitcoin reached as high as $58,000 with a market capitalization of just over $1 trillion before correcting roughly 25% to around $43,000 intraday, one of the two fundamental headwinds cited was that the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust (GBTC) had lost its premium to net asset value and was in fact trading at a slight discount. GBTC had been the biggest buyer of bitcoin in 2020, both for long exposure and for a market-neutral arbitrage trade in which accredited investors and institutions bought at NAV with a six-month lock-up, shorted bitcoin elsewhere, and later sold at a premium. That process permanently converted liquid bitcoin into illiquid cold-storage bitcoin, so once the premium vanished, that source of demand ended. Later, a comparable dynamic emerged with crypto asset treasury companies: on November 20th JP Morgan publicized an MSCI announcement (originally made October 10th) that MSCI might de-list Strategy (MSTR) and other crypto asset treasury companies from its indices, a decision to be confirmed in January. Notably, October 10th coincided with a crypto flash-crash involving $19 billion of leveraged liquidations, suggesting institutions may have been de-risking in response to the MSCI news alongside the Trump trade-war escalation. Bitcoin can survive such de-listings because MSTR holds only about 3.2% of all bitcoin and all treasury companies combined hold a relatively low share. However, treasury companies, along with ETFs, were the major source of demand over the past year, and index exclusion would reduce demand for their shares and thus their ability to acquire bitcoin through share dilution. In both cases, prices corrected sharply: from the roughly $1 trillion market cap peak near $58,000 in the earlier instance, and from about $110,000 at the start of November to below $90,000 in the later one, with metrics showing the most oversold conditions in years.

reference: In late 2023, the Treasury increased its share of short-duration T-bill issuance, which met the excess T-bill demand parked in the Fed's reverse repo facility and pulled that money out of the facility and back into the financial system. The reverse repo facility fell below $1 trillion for the first time since 2021, and at that pace the drawdown almost exactly offset the Fed's ongoing quantitative tightening, producing an essentially flat or neutral domestic liquidity environment. By January 2025, the cumulative picture was that the Fed had removed a little over $3 trillion in liquidity since beginning balance sheet reduction in mid-2022, while over $2 trillion that had been stored in the reverse repo facility began flowing back into banks starting mid-2023, leaving a net reduction of about $1 trillion from over-filled levels. Commercial bank cash levels consequently fell from a peak of a little over $4 trillion in late 2021 to a little over $3 trillion, only about $100-$200 billion above the level associated with the March 2023 regional bank crisis, with SOFR spiking above the interest on reserve balances at the ends of Q3 and Q4 as a sign of tight balance sheet space. Reverse repo usage itself had shrunk to as little as $98 billion on December 20th before a quarter-end spike to $473 billion and a fall back to $237 billion, and was expected to keep inching down, suggesting the Fed would likely end its balance sheet reduction around mid-2025 though not imminently. Combined with a strengthening dollar index since the election, these strained global liquidity conditions coincided with corrections in the S&P 500, gold, and bitcoin. Bitcoin had run from about $69k at the start of November to roughly $99k by November 22nd, spiked above $100k and touched as high as $108k in mid-December, then corrected back to around its November 22nd level, consolidating for about a month and a half. This is all kind of wonky but can be simplified as follows. A healthy sovereign bond market has plenty of liquidity (i.e. good trading volumes where even a large entity can buy or sell a ton of bonds without moving the price noticeably), and no problem issuing a sizable percentage of long duration bonds. However, the U.S. sovereign bond market is not very healthy due to such large ongoing deficits combined with the Fed’s ongoing balance sheet reduction. So, yields keep rising and are very volatile, bond liquidity is low, and small banks are being squeezed in the process. So, the Treasury decided to increase its issuance of short-duration T-bills for its upcoming deficit issuance beyond its normal T-bill ratio. This improves liquidity conditions, but around the margins is the kind of thing that emerging markets do when facing debt and currency problems. The big pool of remaining liquidity available to buy Treasuries is the money that is still stuck in the reverse repo facility. All of this reverse repo money basically represents excess T-bill demand, and the Fed maintains the reserve repo facility so that the market doesn’t drive T-bill yields below the lower floor of their interest rate target. In contrast, there isn’t much demand for longer-duration bonds. And so as the Treasury issues more and more T-bills, it helps meet that excess T-bill demand that exists, and money starts to come out of the reverse repo facility and into holding T-bills. The Treasury then spends this money back into the economy and financial system. The reverse repo facility is now under $1 trillion for the first time since 2021: The ongoing drawdown of the reverse repo facility is putting liquidity back into the system, and how fast it is drained partially depends on how many T-bills the Treasury issues as a ratio of their total debt issuance. By increasing T-bill issuance, they continue to draw money out of the reverse repo facility. And at the current pace, it almost exactly offsets the Fed’s ongoing quantitative tightening (balance sheet reduction), to create a neutral domestic liquidity environment. Once it runs out, liquidity problems could become pretty severe and require a change of course by the Fed. Why is this important?
